chmmc-2010-fall-power-01a.title: Answer and a losing configuration
chmmc-2010-fall-power-01a.body:
$\pi(G_1)=4$. With $3$ pebbles, Alice puts one pebble on each vertex except the target; Bob has no move. With $4$ pebbles Bob wins: if the target has no pebble, some other vertex has at least $2$, and a short case check (moving through the two degree-3 vertices, which are adjacent to everything) always gets a pebble to the target.

**Answer: 4**

chmmc-2010-fall-power-01b.title: Answer and a losing configuration
chmmc-2010-fall-power-01b.body:
$\pi(G_2)=6$. Let the shared vertex be $c$, the left triangle $c,T_L,B_L$ and the right triangle $c,T_R,B_R$. With $5$ pebbles Alice places $1$ on $T_L$, $1$ on $T_R$, $3$ on $B_L$, and chooses target $B_R$: Bob can make $B_L\to c$ (leaving $1$ on $B_L$ and $1$ on $c$), or $B_L\to T_L$ (giving $T_L$ two pebbles, then $T_L\to c$), but never gets two pebbles on $c$, so he cannot reach $B_R$. With $6$ pebbles Bob can always win.

**Answer: 6**

chmmc-2010-fall-power-01c.title: Answer and a losing configuration
chmmc-2010-fall-power-01c.body:
$\pi(G_3)=8$. With $7$ pebbles Alice puts all of them on one vertex and picks the opposite vertex (distance $3$) as target. By the weight argument the initial weight is $7/8<1$, so Bob loses. (In general $\pi(C_n)=2^{n/2}$ for even $n$, see problem 4b.)

**Answer: 8**

chmmc-2010-fall-power-01d.title: Answer and a losing configuration
chmmc-2010-fall-power-01d.body:
$\pi(G_4)=8$ ($=n+1$ for the star on $n=7$ vertices; see problem 7a). With $7$ pebbles Alice picks a leaf as target, puts $3$ pebbles on another leaf, and $1$ pebble on each of the four remaining leaves. The only possible move is from the leaf with $3$ pebbles to the centre, which leaves one pebble on the centre; Bob cannot continue.

**Answer: 8**

chmmc-2010-fall-power-02.title: Pigeonhole
chmmc-2010-fall-power-02.body:
With $n-1$ pebbles Alice places one on every vertex except the target $v$; Bob has no move. With $n$ pebbles, either every vertex has a pebble (including the target), or some vertex has at least $2$ pebbles; since every vertex is adjacent to the target, Bob moves one pebble from it to the target. So $\pi(K_n)=n$.

**Answer: $\pi(K_n)=n$**

chmmc-2010-fall-power-03.title: A losing configuration
chmmc-2010-fall-power-03.body: Take $n-1$ pebbles. Alice chooses any vertex $v$ as the target and puts one pebble on each of the other $n-1$ vertices. No vertex has two pebbles, so Bob has no legal move and does not win. Hence $\pi(G)>n-1$, i.e. $\pi(G)\ge n$. ∎

chmmc-2010-fall-power-04a.title: Lower bound by weights, upper bound by induction
chmmc-2010-fall-power-04a.body:
*Weight argument (used below):* give a pebble on a vertex at distance $d$ from the target the weight $2^{-d}$. A pebbling move never increases the total weight (two pebbles at distance $d$ become one pebble at distance $d\pm1$ or $d$, weight $2^{1-d}\ge$ new weight), and a pebble on the target has weight $1$, so Bob can win only if the initial weight is at least $1$.

*Lower bound.* Put $2^{n-1}-1$ pebbles on $v_1$ and take $v_n$ as the target (distance $n-1$): the weight is $\frac{2^{n-1}-1}{2^{n-1}}<1$, so Bob loses.

*Upper bound.* We show by induction that $2^{n-1}$ pebbles suffice on $P_n$ (the case $n=1$ is trivial). By symmetry assume the target is not $v_n$. Suppose $v_n$ has $a\le2^{n-1}$ pebbles. Bob moves $\lfloor a/2\rfloor$ times from $v_n$ to $v_{n-1}$. The number of pebbles on $v_1,\dots,v_{n-1}$ is then $2^{n-1}-a+\lfloor a/2\rfloor=2^{n-1}-\lceil a/2\rceil\ge2^{n-1}-2^{n-2}=2^{n-2}$. These vertices form a copy of $P_{n-1}$ containing the target, so by induction Bob wins. ∎

**Answer: $\pi(P_n)=2^{n-1}$**

chmmc-2010-fall-power-04b.title: Weights and two arcs
chmmc-2010-fall-power-04b.body:
*Weight argument (used below):* give a pebble on a vertex at distance $d$ from the target the weight $2^{-d}$. A pebbling move never increases the total weight (two pebbles at distance $d$ become one pebble at distance $d\pm1$ or $d$, weight $2^{1-d}\ge$ new weight), and a pebble on the target has weight $1$, so Bob can win only if the initial weight is at least $1$.

*Lower bound.* Put $2^{n/2}-1$ pebbles on $v_1$ and take $v_{1+n/2}$ (at distance $n/2$) as the target. The weight is $\frac{2^{n/2}-1}{2^{n/2}}<1$, so Bob loses.

*Upper bound.* Let $2^{n/2}$ pebbles be placed, target $v_1$, and $p_i$ pebbles on $v_i$ ($2\le i\le n$). If $p_1>0$, Bob has won. Define
$$S_1=\sum_{i=2}^n\frac{p_i}{2^{i-1}},\qquad S_2=\sum_{i=2}^n\frac{p_i}{2^{n+1-i}},$$
These are the weights counted along the two arcs $v_i\to v_{i-1}\to\dots\to v_1$ and $v_i\to v_{i+1}\to\dots\to v_n\to v_1$. Since $2^{-(i-1)}+2^{-(n+1-i)}\ge2\cdot2^{-n/2}$ (AM-GM, the product of the two terms is $2^{-n}$), $S_1+S_2\ge2^{n/2}\cdot2^{1-n/2}=2$, so one of them, say $S_1\ge1$. Now sweep along the first arc: move as many pebbles as possible from $v_n$ to $v_{n-1}$, then from $v_{n-1}$ to $v_{n-2}$, and so on, down to $v_3\to v_2$. Each move of two pebbles preserves $S_1$, so afterwards $S_1\ge1$ still holds, with $q_i\le1$ pebbles on each of $v_3,\dots,v_n$. Then $\sum_{i\ge3}\frac{q_i}{2^{i-1}}\le\frac14+\dots+\frac1{2^{n-1}}<\frac12$, so $\frac{q_2}2>\frac12$, i.e. $q_2\ge2$, and Bob moves a pebble from $v_2$ to $v_1$. ∎

**Answer: $\pi(C_n)=2^{n/2}$**

chmmc-2010-fall-power-05.title: Two cases
chmmc-2010-fall-power-05.body:
Let $2m$ pebbles be placed.

*Target is $v$.* If $v$ has a pebble, Bob has won. Otherwise all $2m$ pebbles are on $H$. Split them into two groups $A,B$ of $m$ pebbles each. Pick a neighbour $u$ of $v$ (it exists since $G$ is connected). Because $\pi(H)=m$, the pebbles of $A$ alone can get a pebble to $u$, and likewise those of $B$ (use disjoint groups). Now $u$ has two pebbles and Bob moves one to $v$.

*Target is in $H$.* Let $v$ have $s$ pebbles. Bob moves $\lfloor s/2\rfloor$ pebbles from $v$ onto a neighbour in $H$. Then $H$ holds $2m-s+\lfloor s/2\rfloor=2m-\lceil s/2\rceil\ge2m-m=m$ pebbles (as $s\le2m$), and since $\pi(H)=m$ Bob can reach any target in $H$. ∎

chmmc-2010-fall-power-06a.title: Remove a non-cut vertex
chmmc-2010-fall-power-06a.body:
*Lemma.* Every connected graph with at least two vertices has a vertex $v$ such that $G-v$ is still connected. Take a spanning tree $T$ of $G$ and a leaf $v$ of $T$ (a tree with $\ge2$ vertices has at least two leaves); then $T-v$ is a connected spanning subgraph of $G-v$.

We prove $\pi(G)\le2^{n-1}$ by induction on $n$. For $n=1$, $\pi=1$. For $n\ge2$ choose $v$ as in the lemma. By induction $\pi(G-v)\le2^{n-2}$, so $\pi(G)\le2\pi(G-v)\le2^{n-1}$. ∎

chmmc-2010-fall-power-06b.title: Paths are the only extremal graphs
chmmc-2010-fall-power-06b.body:
The path $P_n$ has $\pi=2^{n-1}$. Conversely let $G$ be connected with $n$ vertices, not a path (so $n\ge3$). We show $\pi(G)<2^{n-1}$. Pebbling number cannot increase when edges are added on the same vertex set (every move in a subgraph is also a move in $G$), so we may pass to spanning subgraphs.

*Case 1: $G$ has a spanning tree $T$ that is not a path.* We show by induction that every tree $T$ on $n\ge4$ vertices that is not a path has $\pi(T)\le2^{n-1}-1$. For $n=4$ the only such tree is the star on $4$ vertices with $\pi=5\le7$. For $n\ge5$: $T$ has a vertex of degree $\ge3$, hence at least three leaves. If removing every leaf left a path, then $T$ would be a spider with exactly three legs (one vertex of degree $3$, all other degrees $\le2$) and removing a leaf from a leg of length $\ge2$ would leave a spider again, so all legs have length $1$ and $n=4$, a contradiction. Hence some leaf $\ell$ gives a tree $T-\ell$ with $n-1\ge4$ vertices that is not a path, and $\pi(T)\le2\pi(T-\ell)\le2(2^{n-2}-1)<2^{n-1}$.

*Case 2: every spanning tree of $G$ is a path.* If $G$ had a vertex of degree $\ge3$, extend three of its edges to a spanning tree; this tree is not a path. So all degrees are $\le2$, and $G$ (connected, not a path) is the cycle $C_n$, $n\ge3$. For $C_n$, let $2^{n/2}\le N$ pebbles be placed with target $v_1$. The two-arc argument of 4b ($S_1+S_2\ge N\cdot2^{1-n/2}\ge2$, so one arc has weight $\ge1$ and the sweep along it succeeds) shows Bob wins with $N=\lceil2^{n/2}\rceil$ pebbles, so $\pi(C_n)\le\lceil2^{n/2}\rceil<2^{n-1}$ for all $n\ge3$ (for $n=3$: $3<4$).

Hence $\pi(G)=2^{n-1}$ iff $G$ is a path. ∎

**Answer: exactly the paths $P_n$**

chmmc-2010-fall-power-07a.title: The star
chmmc-2010-fall-power-07a.body:
Let $v_1$ be adjacent to all other vertices and let there be no other edges. It is tight: any two leaves share the neighbour $v_1$.

*$n$ pebbles are not enough.* Alice puts $1$ pebble on each of $v_4,\dots,v_n$, $3$ pebbles on $v_3$, and takes $v_2$ as the target. The only move is $v_3\to v_1$, leaving $1$ pebble on each of $v_3,v_1$ and nothing more can be done.

*$n+1$ pebbles are enough.* If the target is $v_1$: either it has a pebble or some other vertex has at least $2$ pebbles; move one of them to $v_1$. Otherwise the target is (by symmetry) $v_2$. If $v_1$ has at least $2$ pebbles, move one to $v_2$. If $v_1$ has exactly $1$ pebble, then $n$ pebbles sit on the $n-2$ vertices $v_3,\dots,v_n$, so one of them has $\ge2$; move a pebble from it to $v_1$, then two pebbles on $v_1$ move one to $v_2$. If $v_1$ is empty, all $n+1$ pebbles are on $v_3,\dots,v_n$. If some $v_i$ has $\ge4$ pebbles, move two pebbles from it to $v_1$ and then one to $v_2$. If two of these vertices have $\ge2$ pebbles each, move one pebble from each to $v_1$ and then one to $v_2$. Otherwise one vertex has at most $3$ and all others at most $1$, so there are at most $3+(n-3)=n<n+1$ pebbles, a contradiction. Hence Bob always wins and $\pi=n+1$. ∎

chmmc-2010-fall-power-07b.title: Cover by stars
chmmc-2010-fall-power-07b.body: Let $2n$ pebbles be placed and let $v$ be the target; if $v$ has a pebble we are done. Let $u_1,\dots,u_d$ be the neighbours of $v$ ($d\ge1$ as $G$ is connected) and $w_1,\dots,w_{n-1-d}$ the other vertices. By tightness each $w_j$ is adjacent to some $u_i$; assign each $w_j$ to one such $u_i$, and let $A_i$ be the set assigned to $u_i$. Then $v$, $u_i$ and $A_i$ span a star centred at $u_i$ with $|A_i|+2$ vertices (use only the edges from $u_i$), whose pebbling number is at most $|A_i|+3$. If every star had at most $|A_i|+2$ pebbles, then the total would be at most $\sum_i(|A_i|+2)=(n-1-d)+2d=n+d-1\le2n-2<2n$. So some star has at least $|A_i|+3$ pebbles; as $v$ has none, these are all on $u_i\cup A_i$ with the target $v$ in that star, so Bob wins within the star, using moves that are also legal in $G$. ∎
